content.text:
<brief>
Create a playful living-garden simulator.

The app shows a small round world with fruit trees, blue blobs, and red blobs. The user can tune the rules, press play, and watch the three groups rise and fall over time.

The experience should feel like a cute animated ecology toy: a little tabletop world with moving bean-shaped characters, visible fruit, live controls, and charts that tell the story of what happened.
</brief>

<freedom>
Use creative freedom. Choose the layout, controls, visuals, algorithms, and technical approach that make the experience strongest.

This prompt gives direction, not a strict checklist. The important part is that the world feels alive, the numbers come from the simulation, and the user can understand cause and effect.
</freedom>

<world>
The world is a round 3D-looking map, like a tiny raised garden dish.

Good visual direction:

- A circular map the user can drag to rotate.
- Trees or bushes with green fruit.
- Blue glossy oval blobs with simple faces.
- Red glossy oval blobs with simple faces.
- Soft shadows, depth, bouncing, blinking, leaning, and small personality.
- Click a blob to inspect it.

Food should look attached to plants. When a blob uses fruit, the plant should visibly have less fruit, then slowly grow fruit again later.
</world>

<simulation>
Each blue and red blob has energy.

Energy changes over time:

- Moving uses energy.
- Waiting uses a little energy.
- Blue blobs restore energy from fruit.
- Red blobs restore energy after a gentle contact interaction with blue blobs.
- Making a new blob uses stored energy, so group size cannot grow for free.
- Fruit returns slowly after being used.

These simple rules should create natural waves:

- More fruit helps blue blobs grow.
- More blue blobs helps red blobs grow.
- Too many red blobs lowers the blue group.
- If blue blobs become rare, red blobs run low on energy and fade.
- With balanced settings, the blue and red groups should rise and fall out of phase.

Do not fake the chart curves. The waves should come from the energy rules.
</simulation>

<motion>
The blobs should visibly choose what they are doing.

Blue blobs can look for fruit, gather near trees, wander, avoid crowded areas, or move away from nearby red blobs.

Red blobs can look for blue blobs, wander when none are nearby, and pause briefly after a successful contact interaction.

Eating and contact should have short cute animations: a pause, chew, bounce, glow, sparkle, fruit shrink, or energy pulse. These pauses should affect behavior so blobs cannot instantly repeat the same action over and over.
</motion>

<controls>
Give the user controls that feel like tuning a living toy.

Useful controls:

- Fruit growth speed.
- Fruit limit.
- Fruit return delay.
- Blue blob energy use.
- Blue blob speed.
- Blue blob vision.
- Blue blob copy threshold.
- Blue blob eating time.
- Red blob energy use.
- Red blob speed.
- Red blob vision.
- Red blob contact strength.
- Red blob copy threshold.
- Red blob pause time.
- Starting fruit trees.
- Starting blue blobs.
- Starting red blobs.
- World size.
- Random seed.
- Simulation speed.

Include play, pause, step, reset, randomize, and a few presets such as balanced garden, fruit-rich garden, red-heavy garden, fragile balance, and low-fruit garden.
</controls>

<charts>
Show the story with real charts from recorded history.

The main chart should show fruit, blue blobs, and red blobs together on one timeline. Use any readable scaling that keeps all three visible at once.

Helpful extra views:

- A blue-vs-red phase plot.
- A run summary.
- Trait trends if the blobs can inherit traits.

The summary can say things like:

- The garden stayed balanced.
- Blue blobs grew first, then red blobs followed.
- Low fruit kept the garden small.
- One group faded and the world settled into a simpler state.
</charts>

<inspection>
When the user clicks a blob, show useful details:

- Group color.
- Energy.
- Age.
- Current action.
- Speed.
- Sensing range.
- Time left in any eating or pause animation.
- Traits or family info if included.
</inspection>

<quality>
A strong result should demonstrate:

- Long-running waves between blue and red groups.
- A fruit-rich setting where blue blobs grow quickly.
- A low-fruit setting where the whole garden stays small.
- A red-heavy setting where blue blobs dip first and red blobs fade later.
- Group sizes that level out instead of growing forever.

Prioritize believable emergent behavior, clear controls, readable charts, and charming map animation.
</quality>

During setup, configure your app and package scripts to use port 9385, then use that port for runtime verification.
Use pnpm exclusively if dependency installation or package scripts are needed. Do not use npm.
Set the browser title and the primary visible title to your model name, using only identity information already available to you. Add nothing else to either title.
Run the relevant checks yourself. Do not edit files outside the current working directory.

content.text:
The garden simulator is built and running at http://localhost:9385 (a Portly temp job with a 60-minute timeout; `pnpm dev` restarts it). In the balanced preset, blue and red rise and fall out of step for the full 25 simulated minutes I tested, on every seed, and nothing in the curves is faked.

**What I checked:**
- **Types and build:** `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm build` pass.
- **Browser:** headless Chrome shows the title and heading as "Claude Opus 5.5" with no console errors.
- **Performance:** about 60 fps at 20× speed with roughly 250 blobs.
- **Controls:** drag, click-to-inspect, Space/S/R shortcuts and reset-to-apply all work.

**One rule I added beyond the brief.** With only the energy rules, every run collapsed. Strong reds wiped out the blues, weak reds died out by bad luck, and I couldn't tune my way out of it. So each tree canopy now shelters one blue from reds, shown as a little leaf hat.
- When blues are scarce they hide and survive; when they're plentiful most are in the open.
- The waves still come from energy. Moving costs more than waiting (faster costs much more), fruit gives +30, a boop gives red energy, and copying splits stored energy with a 10% loss.
- Reds that are low on energy doze to save it, which helps them survive blue lows.

**How each preset played out (headless runs, 3–4 seeds each, up to 1500 s):**

| Preset | What happens |
|---|---|
| Balanced | Blues peak around 93 at 30s, reds follow around 60 about 70–95s later, and the cycle repeats. Never dies out. |
| Fruit-rich | Blues go from 45 to 112+ in 14s, reds surge after them, then big boom-and-bust swings. One seed in four collapsed completely. |
| Red-heavy | Blues dip first (to about 17), then reds drop by half and both settle into waves. Reds usually decline rather than vanish. |
| Fragile | Deep swings with small groups, but it persists. |
| Low-fruit | Blues stay around 10–20, and reds starve out within about 100s. |

**The app itself:**
- **World:** a terracotta dish you can drag to rotate (scroll zooms). Trees carry green fruit that shrinks when picked and slowly regrows. Blobs hop, blink, chew, sweat when fleeing and glow after a boop; birth, eat and boop effects play as particles.
- **Inspector:** shows energy against the copy threshold, age, current action and why, speed now and at max, sensing range, time left on eating or pause, inherited genes, generation, family line, and how the blob died. The selected blob's sensing range and current target are drawn on the ground.
- **Charts:** a timeline of fruit, blue and red (blobs on the left axis, fruit on the right, with hover values), a blue-vs-red phase loop, and inherited speed and vision trends.
- **Run summary:** generated from the recorded history, e.g. "Blue blobs grew first (peak 93 at 34s), then red blobs followed…", "4 waves so far…", "Low fruit kept the garden small…".

**Caveats:**
- Starting trees, starting blobs, world size and seed only apply on Reset; the button pulses "Reset to apply" when they've changed.
- Inherited speed and vision are capped at 80–125% of the slider value. Reds still drift toward the faster end over long runs, and the traits chart shows it.
- A seed reproduces the same run in the browser, but the headless test runner can diverge slightly on knife-edge runs, so its numbers won't always match the browser exactly.
- I lowered the default boop strength to 30 and red copy threshold to 70, so blues and reds end up at similar sizes; with stronger reds they outnumbered blues about 3 to 1.

The main code is in `src/sim.ts`, `src/render.ts`, `src/charts.ts`, `src/analysis.ts` and `src/main.ts`. `scripts/tune.ts` and `scripts/summaries.ts` rerun the preset checks without a browser.Neither notification needs any follow-up.

- **First tuning run (the "error"):** I stopped it on purpose because it was writing its output outside the project folder. I deleted that stray file at the same time.
- **Second tuning run:** this was the same check, writing to `.tune/out.txt` inside the project. It finished, and I already used its results when tuning the simulation.

The app is still running at http://localhost:9385.
